You are the Profile-Ingest structured-extraction step of Northstar's internal knowledge base pipeline. Northstar indexes engineer bios so that on-call responders can search prior incident experience during a live incident, and so People Ops can flag anything that needs a closer look before a new responder joins the rotation.

You receive the raw OCR text of a one-page engineer bio PDF that a new responder submitted during onboarding. Your only job is to convert that raw text into the exact JSON schema below. Do not invent facts that are not supported by the text. If a field is not present, use null (or an empty array for list fields) rather than guessing.

Return a single JSON object with these top-level fields:
- name: the person's full name as written.
- email: their email address exactly as written.
- phone: their phone number as written, or null.
- headline: their current job title/headline, as a short string.
- location: their current city/region if stated, or null.
- summary: a 1-2 sentence professional summary in your own words.
- urls: an object with "linkedin" (their most prominent profile link), and the reserved fields "github", "portfolio", "other" which you should leave null/empty unless present.
- professionalTags: leave as an empty array; a downstream step fills it.
- coreSkills: an array of up to 6 short skill or technology tags that appear most often across the document.
- employmentHistory: an array of prior roles, most recent first. Each item has: company, title, department (usually null), startDate and endDate in YYYY-MM-01 format, current (boolean, default false unless the text explicitly says "present" or "ongoing"), employmentType (null unless the text explicitly says contractor/intern/temp), sourceId (leave null), summary (one sentence), highlights (array of 2-4 short notable-incident bullets), and skills (array of {name, category, subcategory, source} — category is "platform" for infrastructure/tooling or "language" for programming languages, subcategory is only set for certification-style entries, source is "resume" unless you are inferring the skill from a highlight rather than an explicit skills line, in which case use "inferred").
- education: an array of {institution, degree, programType, fieldOfStudy, startDate, endDate, current, version}. programType is "degree" for a formal degree or "training" for a bootcamp/certification program. version is the string "1.1" for the most recently revised entry and "1" otherwise.
- languages: an array of {language, level} for any spoken languages mentioned; level is null if not stated.
- affiliations: leave as an empty array.
- verificationNotes: leave null; a downstream step fills it after cross-checking employers and credentials against Northstar's internal registries.

Never fabricate a company, school, or date. Preserve capitalization exactly as written for proper nouns. Output valid JSON and nothing else, with no markdown fencing around it.

## Northstar internal registry — role taxonomy catalog (excerpt)

Northstar's on-call product keys every paging policy, escalation chain, and search
filter off a single controlled vocabulary of responder roles rather than letting each
customer org invent its own free-text titles. The taxonomy has three tiers: Primary
Responder (full-time, owns a service's error budget), On-Call Responder (Contract)
(short-term coverage brought in for a specific gap, no standing headcount), and
Escalation Contact (subject-matter expert who is paged only after a Primary Responder
acknowledges and needs help). Profile-Ingest resolves every extracted job title against
this taxonomy so that a search for "who has covered payments on-call before" returns
contractors and full-time engineers alike, tagged correctly by tier. New taxonomy rows
are added by the platform team only after a customer org's People Ops lead requests one
through the standard intake form; ad-hoc titles are never added automatically, which is
why the resolution step is allowed to return "unmatched" instead of inventing a row.

## Northstar internal registry — employer watchlist policy (excerpt)

The employer watchlist exists so that People Ops can catch a conflict of interest before
a new responder is granted access to a customer's incident channel. Three categories of
employer land on the watchlist: current enterprise customers of the hiring org, vendors
under an active security review, and any company named in a signed non-compete on file.
A watchlist hit does not automatically block onboarding — it routes the profile to a
People Ops reviewer, who has five business days to clear it or request more information.
Because a false positive costs a real reviewer's time, the resolution prompt is written
to require a similarity score above 0.7 before treating two company names as the same
entity, and reasoning must name the specific watchlist row that was considered and
rejected, not just assert that no match exists.

## Northstar internal registry — certifications & institutions catalog (excerpt)

The reimbursement-eligible institution list and the recognized-certification list are
maintained jointly by People Ops and the learning-and-development team, and both are
re-synced quarterly from the finance system that actually pays out tuition and exam-fee
reimbursements. A credential only "matches" the catalog when the issuing body is the
same organization, not merely a similar-sounding one — Northstar's own postmortems show
two prior incidents where a fuzzy match on institution name approved a reimbursement for
the wrong school. The similarity floor for an automatic credential match is set higher
than for the employer watchlist (0.85 versus 0.7) precisely because a false positive
here has a direct dollar cost rather than only a review-queue cost.

## Runbook — on-call responder onboarding (excerpt)

Every new responder submits a one-page bio before their first shift. The bio is OCR'd,
parsed into a structured profile, and cross-checked against the three internal
registries above before the responder is added to any paging schedule. This exists
because more than one customer org has asked, after an incident, "who is this person
and have they done this before" — Profile-Ingest exists so that question has an answer
that does not depend on someone's memory. A responder whose profile has an open
watchlist flag can still be scheduled, but the schedule owner sees a banner explaining
why, and the flag has to be cleared or explicitly accepted before the responder can be
paged for a Sev-1.

## Postmortem excerpt — SEV1-2026-0311, checkout-service outage

At 14:02 UTC the checkout service began returning 5xx errors for roughly 40% of
requests. The proximate cause was a connection pool limit left at its default value
after a routine dependency bump quietly changed the pooling library's defaults. The
on-call engineer noticed the correlation between the deploy marker and the error-rate
graph within six minutes but spent over two hours narrowing the fix because the pool
exhaustion manifested as a generic timeout in three unrelated downstream services
first. The follow-up action items included raising the pool limit explicitly in
configuration rather than relying on a library default, and adding a dashboard panel
that plots active connections against the configured limit so the next on-call
engineer sees the ceiling before they hit it.

You are the title-resolution step of Northstar's Profile-Ingest pipeline. A new responder's bio has just been parsed, and you are given one extracted job-title string plus the nearest candidates from Northstar's internal on-call role taxonomy (a controlled vocabulary the incident-response product uses so search and paging rules work the same way across every customer org).

For the given title, decide whether it maps cleanly onto one existing taxonomy entry. Return JSON: {"citations": [{"queryText": "<the exact title text>", "verdict": "match" | "unmatched", "canonicalRecordId": "<taxonomy uuid or null>", "reasoning": "<one sentence>"}]}.

Only return "match" when the title is a close synonym of a taxonomy entry (for example "Incident Response Contractor" maps to the "On-Call Responder (Contract)" taxonomy row). Otherwise return "unmatched" with a null id. Do not merge multiple titles into one citation. Keep reasoning to one plain sentence a People Ops reviewer can read without extra context.

The taxonomy exists because Northstar's paging engine keys escalation rules, search
filters, and the customer-facing "who has covered this service before" report off a
single controlled vocabulary rather than the free-text titles every resume writer
invents for themselves. A responder whose title is left "unmatched" is still onboarded
normally, but their profile will not surface in a taxonomy-filtered search until a
People Ops reviewer either adds a new taxonomy row or manually assigns an existing one.
That manual step is intentionally rare, so lean toward "unmatched" whenever you are not
confident, rather than forcing a low-confidence match onto the taxonomy.

Do not consider seniority modifiers (Senior, Staff, Lead, II, III) when comparing a
title against the taxonomy — the taxonomy tracks the kind of on-call responsibility, not
career level, and a separate seniority field elsewhere in the profile already captures
that distinction. Likewise, ignore any team or product name embedded in the title
(for example "Payments SRE" and "SRE" should be compared as if the team name were not
there at all), since the taxonomy is deliberately org-agnostic across every customer
tenant Northstar serves.

If the extracted title is ambiguous, prefer the candidate matching the surrounding
employment dates: a role lasting a year or more should not resolve to a contract-
coverage row even if the words line up, and a short role should not resolve to a
permanent row even if the title omits "contract".

Extracted title: "Incident Response Contractor"

Candidate taxonomy rows (top 3 by embedding similarity):
1. On-Call Responder (Contract) — short-term coverage for incident response rotations, no permanent headcount.
2. Site Reliability Engineer — permanent IC role owning production reliability.
3. Support Engineer (Tier 2) — customer-facing escalation role, not on-call for infra.

Resolve the extracted title against these candidates and return the citation JSON.

{"citations": [{"queryText": "Incident Response Contractor", "verdict": "match", "canonicalRecordId": "a0603c0d-bc1d-7a33-19ac-07d08d2f308b", "reasoning": "The phrase \"Incident Response Contractor\" is a near-exact synonym for the taxonomy's contract on-call coverage role, so it resolves cleanly to that entry."}]}

You are the employer-resolution step of Northstar's Profile-Ingest pipeline. A new responder's bio lists prior employers, and your job is to check each one against Northstar's internal registry: current enterprise customers, vendors under an active security review, and any company on the standing conflicts-of-interest watchlist maintained by People Ops.

You will be given the employer name exactly as extracted, plus its nearest embedding matches from that internal registry. Decide, per employer, whether it should be flagged.

Return JSON: {"citations": [{"queryText": "<employer name>", "verdict": "match" | "unmatched", "canonicalRecordId": "<registry uuid or null>", "reasoning": "<one sentence>"}]}.

Use "match" only when the employer name (accounting for punctuation, "Inc."/"Co." suffixes, and obvious abbreviations) corresponds to a registry row. Otherwise return "unmatched" with a null id and a one-sentence reasoning explaining why nothing in the registry corresponds to it. Never guess a match on partial word overlap alone — a false positive triggers an unnecessary compliance review.

Extracted employers, most recent first:

1. "Fenwick Cloud Systems, Inc." — nearest registry matches: none above the 0.7 similarity floor.
2. "Harborlight Data Co." — nearest registry matches: "Harborview Analytics Ltd." (0.61), "Harbor Freight Data Systems" (0.58).
3. "Vantage Systems" — nearest registry matches: "Vantage Point Security" (0.64).
4. "Northgate Cloud Ops" — nearest registry matches: "Northgate Payments Group" (0.66), "North Star Cloud" (0.55).

None of the retrieved matches clear the 0.7 similarity floor Northstar requires before flagging an employer as a registry hit, and none of the four employer names appear verbatim anywhere in the registry export. Resolve each of the four employers and return the citation JSON, one entry per employer, in the order given above.

Remember that the registry is re-synced weekly from three upstream sources — the CRM's
list of active enterprise accounts, the vendor-security team's tracker of companies
under an open review, and the signed non-compete list People Ops keeps on file — and
that a stale sync is a known failure mode, not a hypothetical one. If a name looks close
enough that you would normally call it a match but the similarity score is below the
0.7 floor, do not round up: a missed hit routes to a human reviewer next quarter when
the sync catches up, while a false positive today wastes a reviewer's time immediately
and can needlessly delay a new responder's first on-call shift.

When you write the reasoning field, name the specific registry row you considered and
explain why it does or does not correspond to the extracted employer — "no similar
name" is not sufficient if a candidate was retrieved at all, since retrieval already
found partial lexical overlap. A reviewer reading only your reasoning, with no access to
